competition: Chile National Mathematical Olympiad — Senior Final (Nivel Mayor)

problems.problem: Writing $1989$ in base $b$ gives a three-digit number $xyz$, so $$1989=xb^2+yb+z,$$ where $b$ is a positive integer, $0<x\le b-1$ and $0\le y,z\le b-1$. The sum of its digits is the same in base ten and in base $b$: $x+y+z=1+9+8+9$. Find $x,y,z,b$.

A rectangle with positive integer side lengths $m,n$ is divided into $mn$ unit squares. Find the number of these squares traversed by a diagonal of the rectangle, excluding squares touched only at a vertex.

Semicircles are drawn on the sides of a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$, as in the figure. The two shaded lunes have areas $X,Y$. Calculate $X+Y$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1989_p3_fig.png

A bank vault has $N$ locks, all of which must be opened to open the vault. Each of five executives has some of the keys, in such a way that any three executives together can open the vault, but no pair can do so. Find the smallest possible value of $N$.
The three side lengths of triangle $ABC$ are rational numbers. Its altitude $CD$ divides side $AB$ into segments $AD$ and $DB$. Prove that $AD$ and $DB$ have rational lengths.
For integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$, define $f(n)$ by $f(0)=2$ and $$(f(n+1)-1)^2+(f(n)-1)^2=2f(n)f(n+1)+4,$$ taking the largest possible value at each step. Find $f(n)$.

A king wishes to keep only the wisest of three sages alive. He places a hat on each without letting its wearer see its colour. They know that the hats were selected from three white and two red hats. They can see one another but cannot communicate; only the first to identify the colour of his own hat will survive. After a long pause, one sage says, “I know the colour of my hat.” What colour is it, how did he deduce it, and what colours are the other hats?
Prove that every triangle can be subdivided into isosceles triangles.
Find all odd positive integers with the same Euler totient as $1990$.

Assigning $0,1,2,3,4$ to the vertices of a pentagon gives each side a weight equal to the sum of its endpoint values. The figure shows an assignment whose side weights form an arithmetic progression. (a) Assign $0,1,\ldots,8$ to the vertices of a nine-sided polygon so that the side weights form an arithmetic progression. Generalise to polygons with an odd number of sides. (b) Prove that, when $n$ is even, no assignment of $0,1,\ldots,n-1$ to an $n$-gon has side weights forming an arithmetic progression.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1990_p3_fig.png
A function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $g(x)\le x$ for every real $x$ and $g(x+y)\le g(x)+g(y)$ for every pair of real numbers $x,y$. Find $g(1990)$.

It is known that the partial sums $1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots+\frac1n$ exceed any prescribed value for sufficiently large $n$. Find a positive integer $n$ such that $$996\le1+\frac12+\frac13+\cdots+\frac1n.$$

A regular polygon is inscribed in a circle of radius $R$ and has apothem $A$. Find the circumradius $r$ and apothem $a$ of a regular polygon of the same perimeter and twice as many sides. The apothem is the distance from the centre to the midpoint of a side.

Decipher a code $C_1C_2C_3C_4$, each position being one of white (W), blue (B), red (R), green (G), black (K), or brown (N); repetitions are allowed. Four guesses give this information: K B G W: two correct colours in wrong positions; R W B N: two correct colours in wrong positions and one correct colour in the correct position; B N R N: two correct colours in wrong positions; G R W B: two correct colours in wrong positions and one correct colour in the correct position. Find all codes compatible with this information.
Find all positive integers $n$ for which $2^n+5$ is a perfect square, that is, equals $m^2$ for some positive integer $m$.

For a finite set $S$ of positive integers, let $\Pi(S)$ be the product of its elements, with $\Pi(\varnothing)=1$. If $S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_k$ are all subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$, including the empty set, where $k=2^n$, find $$\frac1{\Pi(S_1)}+\frac1{\Pi(S_2)}+\cdots+\frac1{\Pi(S_k)}.$$

Consider the ordered sequence $$\frac11,\frac21,\frac12,\frac31,\frac22,\frac13,\frac41,\frac32,\frac23,\frac14,\ldots,\frac1{1992}.$$ Determine how many times the value $1/2$ occurs and at which positions.
Given three parallel lines, prove that there are three points, one on each line, forming an equilateral triangle.

In triangle $ABC$, let $M,I,H$ be the feet of the median, internal angle bisector and altitude from $A$, respectively. Suppose $BC=2$, $MI=2-\sqrt3$, $MH=1/2$, and $AB>AC$. Prove that $I$ lies between $M,H$. Find $AB^2-AC^2$, determine $AB/AC$, and find all side lengths and angles of the triangle.

A mathlon has $M$ athletics events. Only $A,B,C$ participated. In each event first, second and third places earned positive integer scores $p_1>p_2>p_3$, respectively. Their final totals were $22$ for $A$, $9$ for $B$, and $9$ for $C$. $B$ won the $100$ metres. Find $M$ and determine who came second in the high jump.

An $n\times n$ magic square uses $1,2,\ldots,n^2$ so that every row, every column and each of the two diagonals have the same sum $S$. For example, $$\begin{pmatrix}1&15&14&4\\12&6&7&9\\8&10&11&5\\13&3&2&16\end{pmatrix}$$ has $S=34$. Find $n$ for which $S$ differs as little as possible from $1992$, and construct the magic square or describe its construction.

A railway line is divided into ten sections by stations $E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_{11}$. The distance from the first station to the last is $56$ km. A journey over two consecutive sections never exceeds $12$ km, and a journey over three consecutive sections is at least $17$ km. Show that the distance between $E_2$ and $E_7$ can be determined exactly, and find it.
Prove that any triangle can be cut into pieces which can be rearranged to form a rectangle.
Let $x$ be the integer consisting of $n$ digits, all equal to $1$. Prove that if $x$ is prime, then $n$ is prime.
Consider a box of dimensions $10\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}\times1\text{ cm}$. What, in your opinion, is the maximum number of balls of diameter $1$ cm that it can contain?
Let $x$ be a number satisfying $x+\frac1x=-1$. Find $$x^{1994}+\frac1{x^{1994}}.$$
A quadrilateral is drawn in ink on a transparent sheet of paper and illuminated by a lamp. Prove that the sheet can always be positioned so that the shadow projected onto the desk is a parallelogram.

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle of length $m$ and width $n$, where $m,n$ are positive integers. A ray of light starts at $A$, reflects at an angle of $45^\circ$ from an opposite side, and continues reflecting in this way. (i) Prove that it eventually meets a vertex. (ii) If $m,n$ have no common factor greater than $1$, find the number of reflections before it first meets a vertex.
Let $a,b,c,d$ be integers. Prove that $$(a-b)(a-c)(a-d)(b-c)(b-d)(c-d)$$ is divisible (a) by $4$ and (b) by $12$.

Six arcs of radius $1$ are drawn in a circle of radius $1$, as shown in the figure. Find the area $A$ of the shaded region.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1995_p2_fig.jpg
Let $p(X)=a_0+a_1X+a_2X^2+a_3X^3$ be a polynomial of degree $3$ with integer coefficients, and let $a,b,c$ be distinct integers. Prove that it is impossible to have $p(a)=b$, $p(b)=c$ and $p(c)=a$.
Is it possible to assign the numbers $111,112,121,122,211,212,221,222$ to the eight vertices of a unit cube so that numbers on adjacent vertices agree in at most one digit?

A trainer lines up five lions and four tigers. No two tigers may stand next to each other. In how many ways can the animals be arranged, if lions are indistinguishable from one another and tigers are indistinguishable from one another?
Which of the following rational numbers is greater? $$\frac{1995^{1994}+1}{1995^{1995}+1},\qquad\frac{1995^{1995}+1}{1995^{1996}+1}.$$

Three tangent circles are inscribed in a semicircle of radius $4$, as shown. Let their radii, from smallest to largest, be $r,R_1,R_2$. (a) Prove that $$\frac1{\sqrt r}=\frac1{\sqrt{R_1}}+\frac1{\sqrt{R_2}}.$$ (b) Prove that $R_1+R_2\le8(\sqrt2-1)$. (c) Deduce that $r\le\sqrt2-1$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1995_p7_fig.jpg

A shoe manufacturer advertises: buy a pair of shoes without paying. You go to the factory and pay $20{,}000$ for a pair of shoes, receiving the shoes and ten stamps worth $2{,}000$ each. By selling these stamps you recover your money. Customers who buy stamps exchange them at the factory, together with $18{,}000$, for a pair of shoes and ten stamps, and the cycle continues. How much does the factory receive for each pair of shoes? Can this operation be repeated $100$ times, assuming that no person participates more than once?
Construct a triangle $ABC$ given its circumcircle and the points $D,E,F$ at which the altitude, median and angle bisector from $C$, respectively, meet the circumcircle. Assume $AC<BC$.
Let $n\ge2$ be a positive integer. Given $2n$ points in the plane, no three collinear, what is the maximum number of segments that can be drawn between them without forming a triangle?
Consider $ax^2-bx+c=0$, where $a,b,c$ are positive integers. Suppose its roots are real numbers strictly between $0$ and $1$. Prove that $a\ge5$ and $b\ge5$.

A bakery once advertised a special offer for buying two filled cakes. Each cake could contain up to five fillings chosen from those available. A woman said on the radio that there were $1048576$ different choices for the two filled cakes. How many different fillings did the bakery have?

Two circles meet at $A,B$. Let $P$ be a point of arc $AB$ on one circle. The lines $PA,PB$ meet the other circle again at $R,S$, respectively, as in the figure. If $P^{\prime}$ is another point on the same arc and $R^{\prime},S^{\prime}$ are the corresponding intersections, prove that arcs $RS$ and $R^{\prime}S^{\prime}$ are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1996_p6_fig.png

(a) Let $a,b,c,d$ be integers with $ad\ne bc$. Prove that $$\frac1{(ax+b)(cx+d)}$$ can always be written in the form $$\frac{A}{ax+b}+\frac{B}{cx+d}.$$ (b) Find $$\frac1{1\cdot4}+\frac1{4\cdot7}+\frac1{7\cdot10}+\cdots+\frac1{1995\cdot1996}.$$

Lautaro, Camilo and Rafael attend the same class and take the same examinations. Each mark is an integer at least $1$. Camilo had the highest Physics mark. Their total marks were $20$ for Lautaro, $10$ for Camilo and $9$ for Rafael. No two marks among all the examinations were equal. Find how many examinations they took and who had the second-highest Mathematics mark.
For positive integers $a,n$, let $S=a+a^2+\cdots+a^n$. If $S-1=10k$ for some positive integer $k$, prove that there are positive integers $m,\ell$ with $a-1=10m$ and $n-1=10\ell$.
Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral whose diagonals $AC,BD$ meet at $O$. The areas of triangles $AOB,BOC,COD$ are $1,2,4$, respectively. Find the area of $AOD$ and prove that $ABCD$ is a trapezoid.

Triangular dominoes use the two types of equilateral triangular tile shown in the first figure, each of side $1$ cm and with side values $1,2,3$. They are assembled into an equilateral triangle of side $n$ cm using the usual domino rule: adjacent tiles have equal values on their shared edge. The second figure shows an example for $n=2$. (a) Prove that the sum $S$ of the edge values along the boundary of the large triangle is independent of the arrangement and depends only on $n$; for $n=2$, $S=12$. (b) Find $S$ for every $n$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1997_p4_fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_1997_p4_fig2.png

Three circles $C_1,C_2,C_3$ have the property that the two intersection points of each pair are collinear with the centre of the remaining circle. Prove that the three lines so defined are concurrent.

For a set $C$ of points in space, let $P(C)$ be the set of all planes containing at least three points of $C$. (a) Prove that there is a set $C$ for which $P(C)$ consists of exactly $1997$ distinct planes. (b) Find the smallest possible number of points in such a set $C$.

A university offers seven Mathematics courses, and students may choose whichever they wish. After registration: (a) no two students have chosen the same set of courses; (b) any two students share at least one course; (c) adding one more student would make it impossible to satisfy both (a) and (b). How many students are there? Justify your answer.

Professor David and his wife start together at the bottom of a moving escalator and walk up it, counting the steps they climb. David walks twice as fast: for each step his wife climbs, he climbs two. She counts $21$ steps before reaching the top, while he counts $28$. How many steps are visible on the escalator at any instant?

A closed polygon with finitely many sides and no self-intersections is drawn in the plane. Given a point not on its boundary, describe how to determine whether the point lies inside or outside the polygon.

For a base number $N$, let $N_k$ be the decimal integer formed by repeating $N$ exactly $k>1$ times. For example, $N=25$ gives $N_3=252525$, while $N=783$ gives $N_2=783783$. Prove that $7$ divides infinitely many members of $\{N_1,N_2,N_3,\ldots\}$.
Let $AD$ be an internal angle bisector of triangle $ABC$, with $D\in BC$, such that $AB+AD=CD$ and $AC+AD=BC$. Find the angles of $ABC$.
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that there is an $n$-digit integer $N$ whose digits $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ all belong to $\{1,2\}$ and which is divisible by $2^n$.
A $4\times19$ rectangle is formed by $76$ counters, some white, some blue and the rest red. Prove that there is a rectangle inside the larger one with all four vertices of the same colour.
Consider the equation $$ax(x^2+ax+1)=b(x^2+b+1),$$ where $a,b$ are real numbers with $ab<0$. Suppose it has exactly two positive integer roots. Prove that $a^2+b^2$ is not prime.
(i) How many triangles have integer side lengths strictly between $50$ and $100$? (ii) How many of these have perimeter divisible by $3$?

Prove that the only way to cover a square of side $1$ with finitely many non-overlapping discs is with a single disc of radius at least $1/\sqrt2$. The discs may extend outside the square and may have different radii.

In triangle $ABC$, let $h_a,h_b,h_c$ be the altitudes. The internal bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$, and let $d_a$ be the distance from $D$ to $AB$. Define $d_b,d_c$ analogously. Prove that $$\frac32\le\frac{d_a}{h_a}+\frac{d_b}{h_b}+\frac{d_c}{h_c}.$$ For which triangles does equality hold?
Given a positive integer $n$, prove that $2^{2n}-1$ is divisible by $3$.

Two points $A,B$ are marked on a right triangle made of paper. Using scissors, you may cut along an altitude of the current triangle, remove one of the resulting two triangles without the cutting altitude, and continue the process. Prove that after finitely many cuts you can separate $A,B$, leaving one outside the triangles that remain.

Let $C_1,C_2$ be disjoint circles of equal radius and centres $O_1,O_2$, with $C_1$ to the left of $C_2$. A line $\ell$ parallel to $O_1O_2$ meets both circles. Points $P_1,P_2$ on $\ell$ lie to the left of $C_1$ and to the right of $C_2$, respectively, and their tangents to the corresponding circles form a quadrilateral. Prove that a circle exists tangent to all four sides of this quadrilateral.

Petrol stations lie along a circular circuit. The total petrol stored at them is exactly sufficient for a car to make one complete circuit. Prove that there is a station from which a car with a finite-capacity, initially empty tank can start and complete the circuit, stopping to refuel at the stations.

A six-digit Metro ticket is called lucky if its six digits are distinct and the sum of its first three digits equals the sum of its last three digits. For example, $026134$ is lucky. Prove that the sum of all lucky ticket numbers is divisible by $2002$.

Find all positive integers $n$ for which a $15\times n$ rectangle can be tiled by pieces congruent to those shown in the figure. The constituent squares have side $1$, and the pieces must not overlap or leave gaps.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2002_p2_fig.png

Let $M$ lie on segment $AB$. Construct squares $AMCD$ and $MBEF$ on the same side of line $AB$. Let $N\ne M$ be the second intersection of their circumcircles, and let $N^{\prime}=BC\cap AF$. Prove that $N=N^{\prime}$. Prove also that, as $M$ moves along $AB$, the line $MN$ always passes through a fixed point.
The positive integers from $1$ to $2002$ are placed in a row. Can signs $+$ and $-$ be inserted between consecutive numbers so that the resulting algebraic sum is $0$?

Let $T$ be a triangle whose vertices have integer coordinates. Let $E$ be the number of lattice points on its boundary and $I$ the number in its interior. Prove that its area is $$A(T)=\frac E2+I-1.$$
Find all three-digit numbers $N$ for which the average of the six numbers obtained by permuting its three digits equals $N$.

A convex polygon with sides $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ldots,\ell_n$ is called ordered if, for every permutation $\sigma$ of $1,2,\ldots,n$, there is an interior point $P$ such that $$d_{\sigma(2)}<d_{\sigma(2)}<\cdots<d_{\sigma(n)},$$ where $d_i$ is the distance from $P$ to side $\ell_i$. Find all ordered convex polygons.

Determine whether a chess knight can visit every square of a $4\times4$ board exactly once. The figure shows the eight possible moves of a knight, marked C, on an $8\times8$ board.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2003_p1_fig.png
Find all primes $p,q$ satisfying $p+q=(p-q)^3$.

A rectangle is divided by six vertical and six horizontal lines into $49$ smaller rectangles, as in the figure. Each smaller rectangle has an integer perimeter in metres. Must the perimeter of the large rectangle also be an integer number of metres?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2003_p3_fig.png

Juan disliked the criticism of his classmates published in the school newspaper and began tearing it up. First he tore it into four pieces. Subsequently, each piece he selected was torn into either four or ten pieces. Could he obtain exactly $2003$ pieces this way?
Prove that there is a positive integer $N$ whose decimal representation consists of a string of ones followed by a string of zeros and which is divisible by $2003$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Choose $B_1$ on line $AC$ with $AB_1=AB$ and with $B_1,C$ on the same side of $A$. The bisector of $\angle A$ meets $BC$ at $A_1$. Let $\mathcal P,\mathcal R$ be the circumcircles of $ABC,A_1B_1C$, respectively; they meet at $C,Q$. Prove that the tangent to $\mathcal R$ at $Q$ is parallel to $AC$.

Juan proposes an easy but generally incorrect way to simplify a fraction $M/N$, with positive integers $M<N$: delete matching digits simultaneously from the numerator and denominator. For example, $12356/35789$ becomes $126/789$. Find all fractions $M/N$ with $10<M<N<100$ for which this method gives a correct result.

Juana and Juan each write an ordered list of fractions of the same length. Juana writes $$\frac{1^2}1,\frac{2^2}3,\frac{3^2}5,\frac{4^2}7,\frac{5^2}9,\ldots,$$ and Juan writes $$\frac{1^2}3,\frac{2^2}5,\frac{3^2}7,\frac{4^2}9,\frac{5^2}{11},\ldots.$$ Find the smallest number of fractions each must write so that the sum of Juana's list exceeds the sum of Juan's list by more than $123$.
A triangle $ABC$ has integer side lengths in centimetres, circumradius $65/8$ cm, and area $84\text{ cm}^2$. Find its side lengths.

Consider the $2\times6$ board in the figure. Find the number of paths from $A$ to $B$ along its segments subject to these rules: no point may be visited twice; moves may only be right, up or down; and the path must pass through $C$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2006_p3_fig.png
Let $n$ be a six-digit positive integer that is both a perfect square and a perfect cube. If $n-6$ is neither even nor divisible by $3$, find $n$.

A row of $1024$ closed cupboards is numbered $1$ to $1024$. A student opens cupboard $1$, skips the next cupboard, opens the next, and continues. On reaching the end, the student turns around, opens the first closed cupboard encountered, skips the next closed cupboard, and continues back along the row. The student keeps walking back and forth in this way until all cupboards are open. What is the number of the last cupboard opened?

Let $ABC$ be an acute scalene triangle with $BC$ its shortest side. Points $P,Q$ on $AB,AC$, respectively, satisfy $BQ=CP=BC$. Let $O_1,O_2$ be the circumcentres of $AQB,APC$, respectively, and let $H,O$ be the orthocentre and circumcentre of $ABC$. (i) Prove that $O_1O_2=BC$. (ii) Prove that the lines $BO_2,CO_1,HO$ are concurrent.

A knight on a $16\times16$ chessboard can make only two types of move: two squares right and one up, or two squares up and one right. How many different paths take it from the bottom-left square to the top-right square?
Given a triangle $ABC$, determine the disc of smallest area containing it. Clearly justify your answer.

Aurelio and Bernardo play a game. Aurelio first writes $1$, then Bernardo writes $2$. Thereafter they alternate turns, each choosing either to add $1$ to the previous number or to multiply it by $2$, and writing the result. The first player to write a number greater than $2007$ loses. Determine whether either player can guarantee victory regardless of the other's moves.

Thirty-one guests sit in equally spaced chairs around a round table without noticing the name cards at the places. (a) If nobody is in the correct place, prove that rotating the table can put at least two guests in their correct places without anyone leaving their chair. (b) Give a configuration with exactly one guest in the correct place for which no rotation puts at least two guests in their correct places.

Bob proposes a game to Johanna. The board in the figure is an equilateral triangle subdivided into $256$ small equilateral triangles, one coloured black. Bob places a token at any interior point. On each move Johanna chooses a vertex of the board and moves the token to the midpoint between its current position and that vertex. The second figure shows a move using vertex $A$. Johanna wins if she puts the token inside the black triangle. Prove that she can always win in at most four moves.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2007_p5_fig.png

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB=AC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be any point on the shorter arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of $ABM$. Let $T$ lie inside $\angle BMA$ with $\angle TMX=90^\circ$ and $TX=BX$. Prove that $\angle MTB-\angle CTM$ does not depend on $X$.

Alberto tells Ximena that the Transantiago bus routes to his house have three-digit numbers with non-zero first digit, are multiples of $13$, and have their middle digit equal to the average of the other two digits. Find all these bus route numbers.
Let $ABC$ be a right isosceles triangle with right angle at $A$, and let $P$ be an interior point. Write $a=PA$, $b=PB$, $c=PC$. Prove that there is a triangle with side lengths $a\sqrt2,b,c$.

Find all strictly increasing functions $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that, for all $x\ne y$, $$\frac{2\left[f(y)-f\left(\frac{x+y}2\right)\right]}{f(x)-f(y)}=\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{2\left[f\left(\frac{x+y}2\right)-f(x)\right]}.$$
Every point of the plane is assigned one of three colours. Prove that there is a segment of length $1$ whose endpoints have the same colour.

A lorry driver must cross $800$ km of the Atacama Desert between consecutive petrol stations. The lorry holds at most $50$ litres and travels $10$ km per litre. The driver may leave petrol in cans beside the road. For example, starting with $50$ litres, the driver can travel $100$ km, leave $30$ litres there, and return to the starting point with an empty tank to refuel. The driver arrives at the first station with an empty tank. (i) Can the desert be crossed if the station has $140$ litres of petrol in total? (ii) Can it be crossed if the station has $180$ litres?
It is known that $\pi$ is transcendental: it is not a root of any non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients. Using this fact, prove that $\pi+\sqrt2$ is also transcendental.
Nine points lie in the interior of a square of side $1$. Prove that three of them form a triangle of area at most $1/8$.
Find the difference between the lengths of the longest and shortest diagonals of a regular nonagon of side $1$.
Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{100}$ be positive integers. Find all possible integer values of $$S=\frac1{a_1}+\frac2{a_2}+\cdots+\frac{100}{a_{100}}.$$
Find a positive integer $x>1$ such that every term of $$x+1,\quad x^x+1,\quad x^{x^x}+1,\quad\ldots$$ is divisible by $2009$.

Let $A,B$ be two cubes. Assign $1,2,\ldots,14$, in any order, to the faces and vertices of $A$. Give each edge of $A$ the average of the numbers on the two faces containing it. To each face of $B$, assign the sum of the numbers on the vertices, edges and face of the corresponding face of $A$. If $S$ is the sum of the numbers assigned to the faces of $B$, find its largest and smallest possible values.
Let $n\ge6$ green points lie in the plane, no three collinear. Suppose six of them form a convex hexagon. Prove that five green points form a pentagon containing no other green point in its interior.
Integers $a,b$ satisfy $2a^2+a=3b^2+b$. Prove that $a-b$, $2a+2b+1$ and $3a+3b+1$ are perfect squares.
Determine which is larger: $$10^{10^{10^{10}}}\qquad\text{or}\qquad(10^{10})!.$$
The sides $BC,CA,AB$ of triangle $ABC$ are tangent to a circle at $X,Y,Z$, respectively. Prove that the centre of the circle lies on the line through the midpoints of $BC$ and $AX$.
Integers $m,n$ satisfy $m+n\sqrt2=(1+\sqrt2)^{2010}$. Find the remainder when $n$ is divided by $5$.

Let $L$ be a line in the plane and $B_1,B_2,B_3$ three distinct points on it. Let $A\notin L$. Prove that there are distinct $P,Q\in\{B_1,B_2,B_3\}$ such that the distance from $A$ to $L$ is greater than the distance from $P$ to line $AQ$.
Prove that finitely many equal non-overlapping discs of radius $a/2010$ can be placed inside an equilateral triangle of side $a$ so that the sum of their areas exceeds $\frac{17\sqrt3}{80}a^2$.
Find all positive integers $a,b,c$ with $1\le a\le b\le c$ satisfying $$\frac34=\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c.$$

Let $O$ be the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$, and let $S_A,S_B,S_C$ be the circles centred at $O$ tangent to $BC,CA,AB$, respectively. Prove that the sum of the angle between the two tangents from $A$ to $S_A$, the angle between the two tangents from $B$ to $S_B$, and the angle between the two tangents from $C$ to $S_C$ is $180^\circ$.

Consider the graph of ten vertices and fifteen edges shown in the figure. Prove that its edges cannot be coloured with three colours so that the three edges incident to every vertex have pairwise different colours.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2011_p3_fig.png

A map is to be made showing $30$ distinct cities. The distances between every pair of cities are available, each distance counting as one item of data. Three non-collinear cities are already placed on the map. What is the minimum number of data items needed to complete the map?
What is the minimum number of moves needed for a chess knight to reach the top-right square of a chessboard starting from the bottom-left square?
Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ be all positive integers with at most $2012$ decimal digits, none of which is $9$. Prove that $$\frac1{a_1}+\frac1{a_2}+\cdots+\frac1{a_n}\le80.$$

A person joins Facebook and makes at least one new friend each day for the first $30$ days. At the end of those days the person has made exactly $45$ friends. Prove that there is a sequence of consecutive days during which exactly $14$ new friends were made.
Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB=AC$. Let $D$ lie on $AC$ and $P$ on segment $BD$ so that $\angle APC=90^\circ$ and $\angle ABP=\angle BCP$. Find $AD:DC$.
Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers with $0<a,b,c<1$. Prove that at least one of $$ab(1-c)^2,\qquad bc(1-a)^2,\qquad ca(1-b)^2$$ is at most $\frac1{16}$.
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram of area $1$. Let $E,F,G,H$ be the centroids of triangles $ABC,BCD,CDA,DAB$, respectively. Find the area of quadrilateral $EFGH$.

There are $2014$ marked points in the plane, no three collinear. Draw the line through each pair of marked points. Prove that, among any three marked points, there are two separated by an odd number of these lines.
Prove that $n^3-9n+27$ is not divisible by $81$ for any integer $n$.
Prove that if a quadrilateral $ABCD$ can be cut into finitely many parallelograms, then $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

Prove that, for every set of $2n$ lines in the plane with no two parallel, there are two of the lines that divide the plane into four quadrants, each containing exactly $n$ unbounded regions of the arrangement.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2014_p6_fig.png

A parallelogram $P$ and a point $X$ outside it are drawn in the plane. Using only an unmarked straightedge, construct the point $W$ symmetric to $X$ with respect to the centre $O$ of $P$. An unmarked straightedge allows lines to be drawn through two points but cannot measure distances. Here $W$ lies on line $XO$, is different from $X$, and satisfies $OX=OW$.
Find all prime numbers that have no multiple whose decimal representation ends in $2015$.

Let $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ be $n\ge4$ distinct points on a horizontal line $L$. For each pair $P_i,P_j$, draw the circle with diameter $P_iP_j$. Find the maximum possible number of intersection points of these circles strictly above $L$.

Find the number of distinct values of $$\left\lfloor\frac{i^2}{2015}\right\rfloor,\qquad i=1,2,\ldots,2015.$$ For a real number $r$, $\lfloor r\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $r$.
A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle, with $DA=BC=2$ and $AB=4$. The lines $BC$ and $DA$ meet at $E$, and $\angle AEB=60^\circ$. Find the radius of the circle.

A closed curve with simple self-intersections is drawn continuously in the plane, determining finitely many disjoint regions. Prove that every region can be coloured entirely white or blue so that any two regions whose boundaries share a segment of the curve have different colours. A self-intersection is simple if, in a sufficiently small disc around it, the curve looks like a crossing $\times$.

The positive integer $a_n$ is obtained by concatenating, in increasing order and in decimal notation, all positive integers from $1$ to $n$. Thus $a_1=1$, $a_2=12$, $a_3=123$, and $a_{11}=1234567891011$. Find all $n$ for which $a_n$ is not divisible by $3$.
Given a triangle $ABC$, determine whether there exists an interior point $P$ such that every line through $P$ divides the triangle into two polygons of equal area.

A giraffe is a chess piece that moves four squares in one direction and then one square in a perpendicular direction. What is the smallest $n$ such that a giraffe starting at a corner of an $n\times n$ board can visit every square of the board?
The product $$\frac12\cdot\frac24\cdot\frac38\cdot\frac4{16}\cdots\frac{99}{2^{99}}\cdot\frac{100}{2^{100}}$$ is written as a fraction in lowest terms. What is the last digit of its denominator?
Find all triples $(x,y,z)$ of non-negative real numbers satisfying $$x^2-y=(z-1)^2,\qquad y^2-z=(x-1)^2,\qquad z^2-x=(y-1)^2.$$

Let $P_1,P_2$ be two non-parallel planes in space, and let $A$ lie in neither plane. For each point $X$, let $X_1,X_2$ be its reflections in $P_1,P_2$, respectively. Find the locus of points $X$ for which $X_1,X_2,A$ are collinear.
Is it possible to choose five distinct positive integers so that the sum of any three of them is prime?

Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $1$. Points $P,Q,R,S$ are chosen on sides $AB,BC,CD,DA$, respectively, with $AP=BQ=CR=DS=a<1$. Draw the segments $AQ,BR,CS,DP$. Find the area of the quadrilateral formed at the centre of the figure.

A network of hexagons is formed by $2018$ points as shown in the figure. A bee and a fly play the following game. First the bee chooses one of the $2018$ points and colours it red; then the fly chooses one of the $2017$ uncoloured points and colours it blue. They continue alternately, with the bee colouring an uncoloured point red and the fly colouring an uncoloured point blue. At the end, the bee wins if there is an equilateral triangle with all three vertices red; otherwise the fly wins. Determine which insect has a winning strategy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2018_p3_fig.png

Find all positive integers $n$ satisfying $$\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor=n^2.$$ Here $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to the real number $x$.

Let $\Omega=\{1,2,\ldots,20\}$. A non-empty subset $A$ of $\Omega$ is called sum-free if $x+y\notin A$ for every pair $x,y\in A$, where $x$ may equal $y$. Prove that $\Omega$ has at least $2018$ sum-free subsets.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. The altitudes from $A$ and $B$ meet the opposite sides at $D$ and $E$, respectively, and intersect at $H$. Draw the circle with centre $H$ and radius $HE$; a tangent from $C$ touches it at $P$. Draw the circle with centre $B$ and radius $BE$; a tangent from $C$ touches it at $Q$. Prove that $D,P,Q$ are collinear.

A $3\times3$ square is divided into nine unit squares. Place the digits $1,2,\ldots,9$, one in each cell, so that the absolute difference between digits in cells sharing a side is at most $3$. Find the number of such arrangements. Arrangements differing by a rotation or reflection are counted as distinct.

Javiera and Claudio play on a row of $2019$ cells. Claudio first places a token in any cell. Javiera then chooses a positive integer $k$ with $1\le k\le n$, and Claudio moves the token $k$ cells either left or right, at his choice; this is repeated. Javiera wins by forcing the token off the board. Find the smallest $n$ for which she can guarantee a win after finitely many moves.
Find all positive integers $x,y,z$ satisfying $3^x-5^y=z^2$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle ADC=\angle BCD>90^\circ$. Let $E$ be the intersection of $AC$ with the line through $B$ parallel to $AD$, and let $F$ be the intersection of $BD$ with the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$. Prove that $EF\parallel CD$.
Find all positive integers $n$ for which all the digits in the decimal representation of $6^n+1$ are equal.

The points of the $4\times4$ grid shown in the figure can be vertices of squares. Find the number of distinct squares whose vertices are points of a $100\times100$ grid of points.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2020_p2_fig.png
Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB=AC=10$ and $BC=15$. Points $P$ on $BC$ and $Q$ on $AC$ are chosen so that $AQ=QP=PC$. Find $$\frac{\operatorname{Area}(PQA)}{\operatorname{Area}(ABC)}.$$
Find all triples $(x,y,z)$ of integers satisfying $$x+y-z=6,\qquad x^3+y^3-z^3=414.$$
Consider the sequence $a_1=7$, $a_2=7^7$, and $a_n=7^{a_{n-1}}$ for $n\ge2$. Find the last digit of the decimal representation of $a_{2021}$.

An X-design is an arrangement of the digits $1,2,\ldots,9$ in the shape of an X, as in the example in the figure. A design is balanced if the sums of the numbers on its two diagonals are equal. Find the number of balanced X-designs.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2021_p2_fig.png
Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients satisfying $$4p(x^2)=4(p(x))^2+4p(x)-1.$$

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $DC>AD$, and let $P$ lie on $DC$ with $PC=AD$. Let $Q$ be the midpoint of $DP$. Let $L_1$ be the line through $Q$ perpendicular to $DC$, and let $L_2$ be the bisector of $\angle ABC$. Put $X=L_1\cap L_2$. Prove that if $ABCD$ is cyclic, then $X$ lies on its circumcircle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2021_p4_fig.png
Find all real numbers $x,y,z$ satisfying $$\sqrt{x^3-y}=z-1,\qquad\sqrt{y^3-z}=x-1,\qquad\sqrt{z^3-x}=y-1.$$

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle CAB=60^\circ$. Points $D,E$ lie on sides $AC,AB$, respectively, so that $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and $CE$ bisects $\angle BCA$. Let $I=BD\cap CE$. Prove that $ID=IE$.
The $19$ numbers $472,473,\ldots,490$ are concatenated in some order to form a $57$-digit number. Can any number obtained this way be prime?

A right circular cone is made of wood. The circumference $\Gamma$ of its base has radius $10$ cm, and each point of $\Gamma$ is $20$ cm from the vertex of the cone. A red ant and a termite are at antipodal points of $\Gamma$. A black ant is at the midpoint of the segment joining the vertex to the termite. If the red ant moves to the black ant by the shortest possible path, what distance does it travel?
Is it possible to divide a $21$-sided polygon into $2022$ triangles so that no three of all the vertices are collinear?
Determine whether there is a power of $5$ whose decimal representation begins with $2022$.
Let $n$ be a positive integer such that $n!$ is a multiple of $2023$ but is not divisible by $37$. Find the greatest power of $11$ dividing $n!$. Here $n!=1\cdot2\cdots n$.

In Cartesian space, let $\Omega=\{(a,b,c):a,b,c\text{ are integers between }1\text{ and }30\}$. A point of $\Omega$ is visible from the origin if the segment joining it to the origin contains no other point of $\Omega$. Find the number of points of $\Omega$ visible from the origin.

Let $ABC$ be an equilateral triangle of side $1$. Mark $1011$ points $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_{1011}$ on side $AC$ and $1011$ points $Q_1,Q_2,\ldots,Q_{1011}$ on side $AB$, as in the figure, so as to form $2023$ triangles of equal area. Find the length of $AP_{1011}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2023_p3_fig.png
There are $121$ points in the interior of a square of side $60$. Prove that three of them are the vertices of a triangle whose area is at most $30$.
What is the smallest positive integer divisible by $225$ whose decimal digits are all $0$ or $1$?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle ABC=30^\circ$ and $\angle ACB=15^\circ$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $N$ lie on segment $MC$ with $NC=AB$. Prove that $AN$ bisects $\angle MAC$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/clf_2023_p6_fig.png

Let $f(x)=\frac{100^x}{100^x+10}$. Find $$f\left(\frac1{2024}\right)-f\left(\frac2{2024}\right)+f\left(\frac3{2024}\right)-f\left(\frac4{2024}\right)+\cdots-f\left(\frac{2022}{2024}\right)+f\left(\frac{2023}{2024}\right).$$

A container initially holds two coins, and many more coins are on the table. Vale and Diego alternate turns, with Vale starting. If the container holds $n$ coins at the start of a turn, the player may add $d$ coins, where $d$ is a positive divisor of $n$ and $d<n$. The first player to bring the total to at least $2024$ wins. Prove that Vale has a winning strategy regardless of Diego's decisions.
The altitudes $AD,BE$ of triangle $ABC$ meet at its orthocentre $H$. Let $X,Y$ be the midpoints of $AB,CH$, respectively. Prove that $XY\perp DE$.
Find all real pairs $(x,y)$ satisfying $$(x+1)(x^2+1)=y^3+1,\qquad(y+1)(y^2+1)=x^3+1.$$

At least two tokens each bear a number at most $10$, and the sum of the numbers is $S$. Find all values of $S$ that guarantee that the tokens can be divided into two groups so that neither group has sum greater than $80$.
The integer consisting of a $1$ followed by $k-1$ digits equal to $3$ has $k>2$ digits and is assumed prime. Prove that $k(k+2)$ is divisible by $24$. For example, the number is prime when $k=16$.
